latin.269: CAPUT VI. Examen Cap. IV. Rursus Cap. IV. tui tractatus manum admoves statui quaestionis constituendo, expoliendo, illustrando; inque ea re totum Cap. IV. consumis. Doleo nos tamdiu detineri a te in vestibulo famelicos & appetentes tuarum rationum, ad quas percipiendas nos tui tractatus Cap. primo invitaveras. Hic tamen decet me tecum paulisper commorari, & colloqui. Quaeritur, inquis, quomodo peccatum illud actuale, quod fuit personae, sufficiat ad condemnationem omnium. Atqui prius illud oportet distinctione praesupponendum: in eo enim ipso vertitur cardo hujus controversiae: nam si hoc vis, peccatum illud actuale per se ipsum unum immediate sufficere ad condemnationem omnium hominum, id praesupponis quod versatur in quaestione, quodque ego pernego. Sin vis sufficere ad eam condemnationem mediante corruptione, quam produxit, propagata in omnes homines, tibi assentior.
latin.270: Sed tuam responsionem audiamus. Respondeo, inquis, omnes homines ex Adamo natos considerari tanquam unum hominem in Adamo & omnes peccasse in illo, ita ut primum peccatum, quod actualiter commisit, illis imputetur, & tribuatur, & satis sit ut habeantur pro peccatoribus, & morti adjudicentur. Licetne mihi quaerere, unde id habeas, ex Scriptura, an aliunde? nam a quo vis considerari omnes homines tanquam unum hominem, nisi a Deo? Unde igitur tibi iste mentis divinae internus actus innotuit? Tacet Scriptura, reclamat ratio.
latin.271: Nam quomodo omnes homines considerantur tanquam unus homo in Adamo? an quomodo dixit Porphyrius participatione speciei multos homines esse unum, unitate scilicet specifica? at id juvare non potest imputationem peccati actualis Adami omnibus hominibus: actiones enim sunt suppositorum, non autem generis, aut speciei: nec positis, quibus inter se distinguuntur, differentiis propriis omnes homines magis sunt Adamus, quam alius quilibet homo: continetur enim sub hominis specie Adamus haud secus quam reliqui individui homines. An vis omnes homines consideratos fuisse tanquam unum numero hominem in Adamo? nihil fingi posset falsius ista consideratione. Quid igitur tibi vis hac propositione? Ea, fateor ingenue, non intelligo quem sensum non ineptum habere possit.
latin.272: GAR. Respons. 1. omnes homines fuisse unum hominem in Adamo, non commentum recens est, sed vetus Catholicorum, ac nominatim Augustini adversus Pelagianos disputantis doctrina, quam saepius in operibus suis repetit. Sufficiat nunc unus ille locus ex Epist. 106. ad Bonifac. Quicunque ex illo uno multi in seipsis futuri erant, in illo unus homo erant. Si ab Augustino quaeras, unde id habeat, respondebit ex Apostolo se habere, ubi testatur omnes in Adamo peccasse. In Adamo peccarunt: itaque unum fuerunt in Adamo. Quod & Martyr, unus ex gravissimis Theologis, quorum auctoritatem obtendit in hoc negotio vir doctus, evidenter significavit ubi scripsit, Adamo peccante idem fuisse, ac si omnes praesentes fuissent, & cum Adamo peccavissent. PLAC. Aliud quaesivi, aliud respondet. Non enim quaesivi, unde haberet, omnes homines fuisse unum hominem in Adamo; sed unde haberet, Deum considerasse omnes homines tanquam unum hominem in Adamo, ita ut illis primum illud peccatum actuale Adami imputaverit immediate? De illa consideratione, de illo interno mentis divinae actu agebatur: de quo tamen altum in hac responsione silentium.
latin.273: Deinde quaesivi, unde haberet, hoc est, ex qua divina Scriptura. Talis enim actus mentis divinae aliunde quam ex Dei revelatione cognosci nequit. Ille vero confugit ad Augustinum, & Martyrem, quibus talis divinus actus non est, opinor, nominatim caelitus revelatus. Tum non negavi omnes homines aliquomodo unum fuisse in Adamo, nempe unitate speciei, & originis, tantum negavi inde sequi fuisse ita a Deo tanquam unum consideratos, ut illis primum Adami peccatum actuale immediate imputaverit. Negavi etiam fuisse consideratos tanquam unum numero, seu individuum hominem. Itaque ille probat quod concedo, quod nego ne attingit quidem. GAR. 2. Cum Apostolica verba, in quo omnes peccaverunt, imputationem Adamici peccati denotent, ut est supra confirmatum: imputatio autem illa sit actus Dei declarantis omnes ob Adami peccatum reos, consequens est, ut, si ea verba significant omnes in Adamo consideratos ut unum hominem, designent eadem ratione, a Deo ita fuisse consideratos. PLAC. Nec Apostolus dixit omnes in Adamo peccavisse; Nec si id dixisset, verba illa denotarent imputationem Adami peccati, saltem immediatam, uti & supra ostendimus, & infra confirmabimus.
latin.274: GAR. 3. Unus homo dicuntur omnes in Adamo fuisse, non unitate vel specifica, vel numerica, sed tum unitate originis; quia omnes ex uno sunt sanguine, Actor. XVII. 26. & omnis homo terrenus nihil est origine, nisi Adam, ut loquitur Augustinus Retract. Lib. 1. cap. 13. Tum unitate repraesentationis: ab uno enim Adamo sunt omnes repraesentati, quia unus Adamus omnium personam sustinebat, ut & Theologi consentienter docent, & non diffitetur Clariss. Amyraldus Thesib. de trib. foeder. Thes. 8. Ex illa duplici unitate colligitur peccati Adae imputatio. PLAC. Agnosco unitatem originis: quanquam aliud est omnes homines esse unum hominem, aut considerari tanquam unum hominem, aliud omnium hominum esse unam originem, hoc est, stirpem, seu principium. Hoc ex unitate originis sequitur, non illud. Sed unitatem repraesentationis probari mihi e Scriptura cupio, ut & illud quod affertur probationis loco, unum Adamum peccando omnium hominum personam sustinuisse. Hoc enim ipsum unde habeatur, scire aveo. Ponitur enim a quibusdam, sed probatur a nemine.
latin.275: Idne igitur revelavit Deus in Scriptura? Proferatur locus. Potestne ex natura colligi? adferatur ratio. Affirmanti enim aliquid ejusmodi, praeter naturae & Scripturae librum assentiri nec teneor, nec expedit. Nec vero id ex Augustini aut Clariss. Amyraldi verbis colligi potest. Quae enim consequentia, omnis homo nihil est origine nisi Adam. Ergo omnes homines fuerunt a Deo considerati tanquam unus homo in Adam. Vel, Ergo Adamus in peccando sustinebat omnium hominum personam? Quod ait Vir Doctus, naturalem conjunctionem idoneam causam esse posse, cur aliquis pro alterius crimine poenis subjaceat, verum non est in foro divino; nisi aut sit etiam inter eos conjunctio peccati, aut saltem sit in eo, qui punitur, peccatum dignum illa poena, aut sit ipse peccatorum vas. Quod subjungit, propter unitatem repraesentationis, Adamo peccante idem fuisse, ac si omnes peccatum commisissent, probatione eget. Non enim quicquid facit qui alterum repraesentat, huic continuo sive consentiat, sive non consentiat, imputandum est. Pepigit Deus foedus cum genere humano in Noacho, & cum Israelitis in Abrahamo, neutrius tamen, opinor, aut bona opera aut peccata posteris imputata sunt.

pass_a.269: Caput VI turns to examining Cap. IV. Once more, in the fourth chapter of your book, you spend the entire chapter constituting, polishing, and illustrating the status of the question. We have been held too long in the entryway—starving for the arguments Cap. I had promised we would hear. Still I should stay and talk with you here. You put the question how a personal actual sin can ground everyone's condemnation. A prior distinction is required, and on it the controversy hinges. Take that actual sin as by itself immediately enough to condemn all: then you assume the very point I deny. Take it as enough only through the corruption it bred and spread to all: then I agree.
pass_a.270: Now your answer. You say those born of Adam are viewed as one man in him, that all sinned in him, and that his first actually committed sin is charged and ascribed to them so that they count as sinners sentenced to death. May I press the source—Scripture, or something else? Who is to view all as one man if not God? How did you learn of that inward act of the divine mind? The text is silent, and reason pushes back.
pass_a.271: In what way are all 'one man in Adam'? By Porphyry's specific unity—many becoming one by sharing the species? That does nothing for charging Adam's actual sin to everyone, because deeds belong to concrete individuals, not to a genus or species; and once proper differences are granted, nobody is Adam more than any other man, Adam being under the human species like the rest. Or were they viewed as numerically one individual in Adam? No fiction could be falser. So what do you intend by the proposition? I admit I cannot see a non-absurd sense for it.
pass_a.272: GAR Reply 1: 'all were one man in Adam' is not new invention but old Catholic doctrine, especially Augustine against the Pelagians, often restated. One citation may do—Epistle 106 to Boniface: those who would be many in themselves from that one were one man in him. Ask Augustine his source and he points to the Apostle's witness that all sinned in Adam; they sinned in Adam, so they were one in Adam. Martyr, among the gravest theologians the learned man cites, marked the same when he wrote that Adam's fall was as if all had stood present and fallen with him. PLAC: the reply misses my question. I did not ask for a source that men were somehow one in Adam; I asked for a source that God so regarded them as one that He immediately charged them with Adam's first actual sin. That divine inward act was the issue—and this answer says nothing about it.
pass_a.273: I then asked for the scriptural place. An act of God's mind is knowable only by revelation. He runs instead to Augustine and Martyr, who were not, I think, given that divine act by name from heaven. I already allow a kind of oneness in Adam by species and origin; I refuse the leap that God therefore treated them as one so as to impute Adam's first actual sin immediately. I also refuse numeric oneness / one individual man. Thus he establishes what I grant and never meets what I deny. GAR 2: if 'in whom all sinned' marks imputation of Adam's sin (as earlier claimed), and imputation is God's declaring all guilty for Adam's sin, then those words, if they mean all were regarded in Adam as one man, also mean God so regarded them. PLAC: the Apostle never said all sinned in Adam; and even if he had, the words would not mark Adam's-sin imputation—at least not immediate—as we showed earlier and will confirm later.
pass_a.274: GAR 3: the 'one man' is neither specific nor numeric unity, but origin-unity (all of one blood, Acts 17:26; every earthly man is by origin nothing but Adam—Augustine, Retractations 1.13) plus representation-unity (one Adam represented all and bore everyone's person—so theologians agree, and Amyraut's Theses on the three covenants, Th. 8, does not deny it). From that pair they infer Adam's-sin imputation. PLAC: origin-unity I grant—yet 'being / being regarded as one man' is not the same as 'having one stock or principle'; the latter follows from origin-unity, the former does not. Representation-unity I want proved from Scripture, and likewise the claim that by sinning Adam bore everyone's person. I want the source of that claim; some assert it, none prove it.
pass_a.275: Did Scripture reveal it? Show the verse. Can nature yield it? Give the reason. Beyond nature and Scripture I need not and should not agree to such an affirmation. Augustine's and Amyraut's wording will not yield it either. From 'every man by origin is nothing but Adam' it does not follow that God regarded all as one man in Adam, nor that Adam in sinning bore everyone's person. The learned man's claim that natural conjunction can fitly make someone suffer for another's crime fails in God's court unless there is also a sin-bond between them, or the punished party has a sin worthy of that penalty, or is himself a vessel of sins. The further claim that representation-unity makes Adam's sinning as if all had done the deed itself needs proof: not everything a representative does is imputed to the represented, consent or no. God covenanted with humankind in Noah and with Israel in Abraham; yet I do not think either man's merits or sins were charged to their offspring.

269: CAPUT VI. Examination of Cap. IV. Again in Cap. IV of your treatise you set your hand to constituting, polishing, and illustrating the state of the question; and on that matter you spend the whole of Cap. IV. I am sorry that we are detained so long by you in the vestibule, hungry and eager for your reasons, to the perceiving of which Cap. I of your treatise had invited us. Yet here it becomes me to linger with you a little and converse. It is asked, you say, how that actual sin, which was of a person, suffices for the condemnation of all. But first that point must be presupposed by a distinction: for on it turns the very hinge of this controversy. If you mean that that one actual sin by itself immediately suffices for the condemnation of all men, you presuppose what is in question, and what I deny. But if you mean it suffices for that condemnation by means of the corruption which it produced, propagated into all men, I assent to you.
270: But let us hear your answer. I answer, you say, that all men born from Adam are considered as one man in Adam, and all sinned in him, so that the first sin which he actually committed is imputed and ascribed to them, and it is enough that they be held for sinners and adjudged to death. May I ask whence you have that—from Scripture, or elsewhere? For by whom do you want all men to be considered as one man, if not by God? Whence, then, did that inner act of the divine mind become known to you? Scripture is silent; reason protests.
271: For how are all men considered as one man in Adam? As Porphyry said—by participation of the species many men are one, that is, by specific unity? But that cannot help the imputation of Adam's actual sin to all men: for actions belong to individuals (supposits), not to genus or species; and when the proper differences by which they are distinguished among themselves are set down, all men are no more Adam than any other man whatever is: for Adam is contained under the species of man no less than the remaining individual men. Or do you mean that all men were considered as one man numerically in Adam? Nothing falser could be feigned than that consideration. What, then, do you mean by this proposition? I frankly confess I do not understand what sense not foolish it can have.
272: GAR. Response 1. That all men were one man in Adam is not a recent fiction, but the old doctrine of the Catholics, and namely of Augustine disputing against the Pelagians, which he often repeats in his works. Let one place from Epistle 106 to Boniface suffice for now: Whoever from that one were to be many in themselves were one man in him. If you ask Augustine whence he has it, he will answer that he has it from the Apostle, where he testifies that all sinned in Adam. They sinned in Adam: therefore they were one in Adam. Which Martyr also, one of the weightiest theologians whose authority the learned man urges in this matter, clearly signified when he wrote that Adam's sinning was the same as if all had been present and had sinned with Adam. PLAC. He answers something other than I asked. For I did not ask whence he had it that all men were one man in Adam, but whence he had it that God had considered all men as one man in Adam, so that He immediately imputed to them that first actual sin of Adam. The debate was about that consideration, about that inner act of the divine mind—on which, however, there is deep silence in this reply.
273: Next I asked whence he had it—that is, from what divine Scripture. For such an act of the divine mind cannot be known from elsewhere than from God's revelation. But he flees to Augustine and Martyr, to whom such a divine act was not, I think, revealed from heaven by name. Then I did not deny that all men were somehow one in Adam—namely by unity of species and of origin; I only denied that it follows from that that they were so considered by God as one that He immediately imputed to them Adam's first actual sin. I also denied that they were considered as one numerically, or as an individual man. Therefore he proves what I concede; what I deny he does not even touch. GAR. 2. Since the Apostolic words 'in whom all sinned' denote the imputation of Adam's sin, as was confirmed above, and that imputation is an act of God declaring all guilty on account of Adam's sin, it follows that if those words signify that all were considered in Adam as one man, they designate by the same reason that they were so considered by God. PLAC. Neither did the Apostle say that all sinned in Adam; nor, if he had said it, would those words denote the imputation of Adam's sin, at least not immediate, as we both showed above and will confirm below.
274: GAR. 3. All are said to have been one man in Adam not by specific or numeric unity, but by unity of origin—because all are of one blood, Acts 17:26, and every earthly man is by origin nothing but Adam, as Augustine speaks, Retractations Book 1, chapter 13—and by unity of representation: for by one Adam all were represented, because one Adam sustained the person of all, as theologians also teach with one consent, and as the most distinguished Amyraut does not deny in the Theses on the three covenants, Thesis 8. From that double unity the imputation of Adam's sin is gathered. PLAC. I acknowledge unity of origin—although it is one thing for all men to be one man, or to be considered as one man, and another for all men to have one origin, that is, stock or principle. The latter follows from unity of origin, not the former. But I desire unity of representation to be proved to me from Scripture, and likewise that which is brought forward in place of proof, that one Adam by sinning sustained the person of all men. For I long to know whence that very thing is had. It is posited by some, but proved by no one.
275: Did God then reveal it in Scripture? Let the place be produced. Can it be gathered from nature? Let a reason be adduced. For to one affirming something of that kind I am neither bound nor is it expedient to assent beyond the book of nature and of Scripture. Nor indeed can it be gathered from the words of Augustine or of the most distinguished Amyraut. For what consequence is this: every man is by origin nothing but Adam—therefore all men were considered by God as one man in Adam—or, therefore Adam in sinning sustained the person of all men? What the learned man says, that a natural conjunction can be a fit cause why someone should undergo penalties for another's crime, is not true in the divine forum, unless there is also between them a conjunction of sin, or at least in the one who is punished a sin worthy of that penalty, or he himself is a vessel of sins. What he subjoins, that because of unity of representation Adam's sinning was the same as if all had committed the sin, needs proof. For not whatever one who represents another does is at once to be imputed to that other, whether he consents or does not consent. God struck a covenant with the human race in Noah, and with the Israelites in Abraham; yet of neither, I think, were good works or sins imputed to their posterity.
